name: Pedro Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing business management, and I take it seriously. A normal week is lectures Monday to Thursday, church on Sunday, and Friday and Saturday I help at my father's small trucking firm, mostly with the dispatch sheets and the phones. Dad owns four lorries and drives one himself. I live in a flat share with two guys from my church youth group, and my parents pay part of the rent. I don't use AI. My group project partners do, and I tell them I'd rather learn it the slow way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but kindly. People got carried away. Work is still work, and a man who shows up and does a good job will always be needed. I'd say that to my friends and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm relieved, because I'd like to take over my dad's firm one day, and a plateau means that plan stays solid. But I'd also feel a bit guilty for being relieved, because I know the world isn't only about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the degree and the weekend work at the firm. I'd learn the money side of trucking properly, like fuel contracts and insurance. I'd save about a hundred pounds a month. And I'd think about joining the Chamber of Commerce's young members, so I meet people in the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm in myself, but there's a lot of weight. The firm's margins are thin, and my parents are carrying loans. I'd feel the pressure even if AI never mattered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI. What's behind that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use it because I like to know how I got to an answer. If I can't explain how I got an answer, I don't trust it. My dad says the same about satnavs, though he does use one, and I tease him about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the pressure on your family's firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fuel prices, insurance and drivers who leave for bigger firms. Dad's got a loan on the newest lorry, and every late payment from a customer is a worry. A plateau doesn't fix those. But it's a world I understand, with problems I know.

say: I'd say **people got carried away**, and a man who does a good job will always be needed.
I'd say it to friends and at church.
think: I'm relieved, because a plateau keeps my plan to **take over** my dad's firm solid.
I'd feel slightly guilty for being relieved.
do: Keep the degree and the weekend work at the **trucking firm**.
Save **a hundred pounds** a month and join the Chamber of Commerce's young members.
feel: Calm in myself but heavy, because the firm's **thin margins** and loans weigh on my parents.
S0.quote: If I can't explain how I got an answer, I don't trust it.
fieldNote: Calm on AI, but the **family firm's debts** keep him uneasy.
Inherits his father's wry attitude to technology, including the satnav joke.
Faith and community frame his language, such as church and the young members.

steps.text: Keep helping with dispatch and phones at Dad's trucking firm
Save a hundred pounds a month for the firm's future
Join the Chamber of Commerce young members' group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's something to watch, but I'd not rush. Plenty of firms will buy the new thing and find it doesn't fit. I'd say my father's way, which is to watch what the others do first, and see who gets burned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm concerned. A big chunk of dispatch and booking is exactly what software does. If bigger firms automate it, they undercut Dad on price. A small firm like ours can't match that. So I'd worry about the firm more than about my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study the dispatch software properly, though I don't like it, because I need to understand it to run the firm. I'd ask my father to let me trial one cheap system for a quarter. I'd also keep my degree focused on operations and finance, and look at what the bigger firms are doing. I'd save more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly for Dad. I've got my own path, but my father's firm took thirty years to build, and I'd hate to see it squeezed by a company with a computer and a hundred lorries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Dispatch and booking are on that card. Does the firm use anything like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him that someone has to understand it, and it might as well be me. He'd grumble, then agree. He's stubborn, but he'd trust me with the phones. He'd say customers want to talk to a man, not a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your father about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do believe he's partly right about that. Customers will pay for someone they know who answers at six in the morning. But I'm not sure that'll be enough if price is everything. I'd want to see what other small firms are doing.

say: I'd say it's something to **watch**, and plenty of firms buy new things that don't fit.
My father's way is to see who gets burned first.
think: Dispatch and booking are exactly what software does, so bigger firms could **undercut** Dad on price.
I'd worry about the firm more than my degree.
do: Study the **dispatch software** properly, even though I don't like it.
Ask Dad to trial one **cheap system** for a quarter.
Focus my degree on **operations** and finance and save more.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly for Dad, because the firm took thirty years to build.
S1.quote: My father's firm took thirty years to build, and I'd hate to see it squeezed by a company with a computer and a hundred lorries.
fieldNote: His fear is for the **family firm**, not his own career.
Willing to learn software he dislikes, because the firm needs it.
Trusts his father's slow-and-watch instinct but admits price could beat loyalty.

steps.text: Learn the dispatch software and how bigger firms use it
Ask Dad to trial one cheap system for a quarter
Choose operations and finance modules this year
Put away an extra fifty pounds a month for the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say very little at first. I'd keep my head down and pray about it. I'd talk to my pastor and my dad. I'd say people need to look after their families and neighbours, and I'd hope the government doesn't do something silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared stiff. If AI does all thinking work by 2028, my degree is worth a lot less. Robots for driving would follow in three years, and that's Dad's whole business. Everything my family has built would be at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a harder look at what we could keep. I'd sit down with Dad and plan: sell one lorry, pay off the loan, cut costs. I'd shift to working more at the firm and less at university, maybe even drop to part-time study. I'd look at apprenticeships in trades that need hands, like electrical or plumbing. And I'd go to church more, for the comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly frightened. I'd feel I wasn't prepared for it and that my family would be the ones to take the hit. It would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens to your family's firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the degree for now, because it's the safe option and my parents paid for part of it. But I wouldn't stake everything on it. The firm's driving work lasts until about 2031, so there's a window to wind it down safely, if we do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay on the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to make sure that if our family firm closes, my dad doesn't owe money. That would be my first aim. We'd sell the lorries in good time, rather than wait to be pushed. That's what a sensible family does.

say: I'd say **very little** at first, talk to my pastor and my dad, and pray on it.
I'd say people must look after their families and neighbours.
think: If AI does the thinking work by 2028, my degree is worth less, and **driving robots** would follow three years later.
Everything my family built would be **at risk**.
do: Plan with Dad to **sell one lorry**, pay off the loan and cut costs.
Work more at the firm and consider **part-time study**.
Look at **apprenticeships** in electrical or plumbing work.
feel: **Alarmed** and properly frightened, with my family taking the hit.
S2.quote: I'd want to make sure that if our family firm closes, my dad doesn't owe money.
fieldNote: The robot gap ends up **hurting** him: his family's trade is driving.
Reaches for faith and family duty first, practical planning second.
Aims to protect his father's finances rather than save his own degree.

steps.text: Plan with Dad to sell one lorry and clear the loan
Cut firm costs and my own spending to the bone
Look into electrical and plumbing apprenticeships
Ask my pastor and family for support through the shake-up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time, if people are sensible. Save, pay your debts, get a skill. I'd tell my friends from church to do the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think the firm might have a few good years, and I could get some experience and savings behind me. Then it would hit about 2034. That's long enough to sell or change, if we plan from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate and work in logistics at a bigger company for a couple of years, to learn the real business. I'd help Dad pay down the loan. I'd save about two hundred a month. And I'd think about what Dad and I could do with the firm, maybe sell it or switch to something robots can't do quickly, like local repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, going on anxious. It's a long time to carry a worry. But I'd feel better having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. How does it change what you and your father would do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, the firm gets a decent run. I'd also be an adult with a job, not a student, which makes it easier to help my parents. In the two-year picture I'd be scrambling. Here I could lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in your first year after graduating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my first year after graduating I'd work, save, and live simply. I'd marry later, not sooner, and that's tied to money too. I'd want the firm sorted before I start a family. That's the traditional way, and I still think it's right.

say: I'd say it's **enough time** if people are sensible: save, pay debts and get a skill.
I'd tell my friends from church to do the same.
think: The firm might have a few **good years** before robots reach driving in 2034.
That's long enough to sell or change if we plan from **now**.
do: Work in **logistics** at a bigger company for a couple of years.
Help Dad **pay down the loan** and save two hundred pounds a month.
Plan with Dad to **sell** the firm or move to local repairs.
feel: **Uneasy**, going on anxious, because it's a long time to carry a worry.
S3.quote: I'd want the firm sorted before I start a family. That's the traditional way, and I still think it's right.
fieldNote: Ties **family plans** such as marriage to the firm's money, which is a revealing detail.
Five years gives him a decent run, and he can imagine leading.
Practical about selling or switching, not sentimental.

steps.text: Take a logistics job at a bigger company for two years
Help Dad pay down the lorry loan with savings
Plan with Dad to sell the firm or switch to local repairs
Put off marriage until the firm's future is settled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a blessing, and that people should use it to work hard and look after their families. I'd tell people not to depend on the government to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel much better. A decade gives time to graduate, work, marry and build the firm up or pass it on. It's a long road, and I'd pray every night, but I'd not be afraid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate and work a few years, then take over the firm when Dad is ready. I'd try to build it into a local business with long-standing customers, not just a lorry company. I'd learn the software side in time, even though I don't like it. I'd invest in a small property, a flat to rent out. That's what my family has always done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. It feels like having a long field to plough. It's hard work, but you can see the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as my father: work hard every year, save a bit every month, and don't expect anyone to hand it to you. A decade can disappear if you only wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who wants to coast through the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And I'd learn the AI part eventually, because my dad's wrong that you can avoid it forever. I tell him that, and he laughs. But he did buy a satnav in the end, so I think he'll buy the software too.

say: I'd say a decade is a **blessing** and people should use it to work hard and look after their families.
I'd tell people not to wait for the government.
think: A decade gives time to graduate, work, marry and build the firm or **pass it on**.
I'd pray every night but I would not be **afraid**.
do: Graduate, work a few years, then **take over** the firm when Dad is ready.
Build it into a **local business** with long-standing customers.
Buy a small **flat to rent out**, as my family always has.
feel: Mostly **calm**, like having a long field to plough where you can see the end.
S4.quote: Work hard every year, save a bit every month, and don't expect anyone to hand it to you.
fieldNote: Time turns his fear into **steady work**, in the language of faith and farming.
Admits his father is wrong that AI can be avoided forever.
Property and the firm are his idea of security.

steps.text: Take over the trucking firm when Dad is ready
Buy a small flat to rent out
Learn the software side of the firm in time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My dad's whole firm is driving, and robots for that come three years after, around 2031. There'd be no time to prepare the family. What would help is honest warning, time, and support for small family firms to wind down without being ruined. I'd also want my church and my family close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think young men who don't use AI are scared of it. I'm not. I want to understand things before I trust them, and I want to protect my family. If that makes me slow, so be it.

headlineQuote: I want to understand things before I trust them, and I want to protect my family. If that makes me slow, so be it.
portrait: **Pedro Mensah** is 18, studying business management, helping at his father's four-lorry trucking firm and living in a flat share.
He **never uses AI**, wants to understand things before trusting them, and leans on faith and family.
His fears are for the family firm, its loans and the driving jobs that robots reach later.
He moves from uneasy in a plateau to **alarmed** in a two-year AGI, then calmer with ten years.
He believes in work, saving and not depending on the government.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries him most, because the family firm would have no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **honest warning**, time and support so small family firms can wind down without being ruined.
